## 01 · Opening · From environmental evidence to performance-aware co-design

*46 words · start by 0:00 · on screen: Title, research identity, and the research map with the proposed PhD territory (three possible directions) drawn faintly.*

Thank you for having me. I am Roman Jahandideh, an MSc student in Interactive Arts and Technology at SFU.

My work asks how AI can help designers explore built environments without losing the rules, the performance evidence and the human judgment that make a proposal accountable.

## 02 · Opening · A proposal is only useful if a designer can check it

*50 words · start by 0:29 · on screen: The question and the GenEnv program, then the route from making to human-AI co-design with one capability carried from each stage.*

AI can already produce convincing massing proposals. But a designer can only use one if they can see which rule it followed, how its performance was calculated, and what was assumed.

I will end with three possible directions within GenEnv’s Human-AI Co-Design program. First, the route that led me here.

## 03 · Background · I learn by making

*37 words · start by 1:01 · on screen: One childhood photograph and one idea: making as a way of understanding.*

I have always learned by making: as a child I took things apart to see how they worked, and my schooling pushed mathematics and science early. I still build something, test where it fails, and revise it.

## 04 · Background · From making things to designing places

*43 words · start by 1:25 · on screen: Tabriz campus; the degree; why architecture.*

That led me to architecture at Tabriz Art University. Architecture let me make new things with real effects on how people live together. I learned to think about space through form, narrative and social purpose, and tested my work in interschool design competitions.

## 05 · Background · Zangar Museum: history translated into space

*49 words · start by 1:53 · on screen: The night render and the concept board: three periods, three forms.*

My dissertation was the Zangar Museum, about the people of Tabriz under three governments across roughly a century. Each period became one sharp, angled form, so visitors read the history through the building itself.

It was supervised by Prof. Parisa Hashempour and named the best dissertation of my class.

## 06 · Background · From narrative to plan and section

*26 words · start by 2:24 · on screen: Plans and section at a readable scale.*

Developing it taught me to carry one idea from a cultural story through geometry, program and circulation, so the plan and section still tell the history.

## 07 · Background · Construction, framing and light

*40 words · start by 2:41 · on screen: One strip: the foldable cabin and the two winning photographs, with the three results as small facts.*

I kept testing ideas in competitions: a foldable cabin for people displaced by disasters, a landscape design, and long exposures of the city at night. Each was about how construction, framing and light change the way a space is experienced.

## 08 · Background · From objects to environmental systems

*42 words · start by 3:07 · on screen: Tabriz and Istanbul side by side: the move from composing objects to reading systems.*

Over time I felt my architecture paid too little attention to society and nature, so I studied landscape architecture at Istanbul Technical University. Landscape taught me that space is also terrain, water, ecology and time. At ITU I also started using GIS.

## 09 · Background · A water system, not an object

*47 words · start by 3:34 · on screen: Analysis, water section and connected units: from site reading to a connected system.*

On Büyükada, a steep island, rainwater runs straight down the streets. The design began from slope, roads and runoff, and became a system of collectors, cisterns and planted basins linked down the hill to shared storage. Design became a network of relationships I could represent and measure.

## 10 · Background · First experiments with generative AI

*52 words · start by 4:04 · on screen: Three of Roman’s own Midjourney images from 2022: an exploratory use of generative AI for landscape and atmosphere, and the limit it exposed.*

During my master’s in Istanbul I also experimented with Midjourney, generating landscapes and atmospheres from text prompts. It was exciting how fast the images came, but they had no scale, no site and nothing I could verify. That limit is part of why I now study AI that stays connected to evidence.

## 11 · Previous research · Designing depth in virtual landscapes

*54 words · start by 4:37 · on screen: Study design redrawn as vectors: four transparency levels, twelve colour conditions.*

In the Virtual Landscape Lab with Dr. Ikhwan Kim, I studied a problem designers face in VR: depth does not always read as intended. Sixty people each made 264 depth judgments. At high transparency the usual rule reversed. The finding is bounded, but it could guide colour and transparency in a VR design tool.

## 12 · Previous research · Learning how AI systems are built and run

*101 words · start by 5:11 · on screen: Why SFU: learning how AI systems are built and run. Capability chain from question to publication, the SFU Surrey atrium and one teaching photo.*

Midjourney showed me what AI could produce, but not how it works. To use AI responsibly in design, I needed to learn how these systems are built and run. That led me to SFU and Prof. Steve DiPaola’s iViz Lab, which works on AI. Alongside the lab, I kept building small architectural systems and prototypes.

There I learned to carry a question the whole way: a prototype in Unity and C#, a data pipeline in Python and JavaScript, then the study and the paper. I also teach as a TA in three SIAT courses, and last week ran a Unity workshop.

## 13 · Previous research · How a representation shapes trust

*74 words · start by 6:11 · on screen: Halo states and BioTerrarium zones; the trust trade-off as the headline, statuses kept small.*

In one study, a remote teammate’s heart rate appeared as a halo instead of numbers. People read it above chance and helped faster, but trusted the numbers more. BioTerrarium is still under revision.

These studies taught me to build a complete research system and examine how people understand, trust and use it. I now want to bring that back into architecture and landscape design, where AI recommendations must stay connected to real performance evidence.

## 14 · Research projects · AI interprets and proposes. Verified code computes. The designer judges.

*43 words · start by 6:57 · on screen: Matrix of the three roles (AI, verified code, designer) across the four projects, each role with its own line style.*

Then I began several small research projects on parts of one problem: how rules become spatial knowledge, how that becomes editable geometry, how constraints are calculated, and how AI might support performance critique. In each, AI proposes, code computes, and the designer judges.

## 15 · Research projects · Zoning Literacy Assistant

*53 words · start by 7:24 · on screen: The retrieve, answer, verify pipeline stopping at “not covered”.*

First, regulation. I explored whether an assistant could answer zoning questions only from cited clauses. Asked how many storeys a laneway house may have, it says the source does not cover it, and stops. It uses ten clauses of one zone. The lesson: urban knowledge has to keep its sources and its non-answers.

## 16 · Research projects · Parametric Massing Generator

*50 words · start by 7:58 · on screen: Rules becoming an editable envelope, plus a captured interface state.*

Second, geometry. Here the AI extracts eight rules from the bylaw, each with its source sentence, and code builds the envelope. Change one value, like the rental condition, and everything that depends on it updates. It is a research prototype, not compliance software. The lesson: AI output should stay editable.

## 17 · Research projects · Vancouver View Corridor Massing

*50 words · start by 8:29 · on screen: Section: the sloped view ceiling, the flat cap, then floor-by-floor trimming with live counts.*

Third, a spatial constraint. Protected views in Vancouver are sloped, but quick checks use a flat cap. Clipping floor by floor against the City’s corridor data gives eighteen floors instead of ten. But the base elevation and slope are placeholders, so the number only means something with its assumptions attached.

## 18 · Research projects · Environmental Massing Agents

*53 words · start by 9:01 · on screen: Agent roles around one evaluator box; search runs against the target, with “not faster” in red.*

Fourth, performance critique. Agents propose and critique; deterministic evaluators score. I expected guided search to be faster. It was not, but it was more reliable: four of five runs against one of five. The models are simplified and the live language-model loop has not run. More agents do not automatically give better design.

## 19 · PhD directions · What already exists—and the missing link

*145 words · start by 9:34 · on screen: Selected existing capabilities with references, attributed Xun Liu, GenEnv and UBC work highlighted in yellow (starting with the earlier XL Studio environmental-feedback work), then a cautiously worded open research problem scoped to the systems reviewed.*

Before defining a direction, I reviewed recent work across computational design, building simulation and human–AI co-design. There is already strong research connecting language models to Grasshopper, generating CAD, running simulations and bringing parametric models into VR.

Reading the earlier XL Studio projects helped me see a longer trajectory in your work. FluX and The Third Simulation brought environmental processes into interactive design feedback; ECO GEN connected ecological data with generative design; and Archi-Agent connected natural-language intent with parametric operations. My proposed directions build on that trajectory by asking how performance evidence, uncertainty and design changes can remain traceable and under the designer’s control.

Across the systems I reviewed, however, I did not find one continuous, human-governed workflow that keeps performance evidence valid and traceable as geometry, assumptions and tool states change. That is the shared problem behind the three directions I will show next.

## 20 · PhD directions · Between the designer’s intention and the final decision

*76 words · start by 11:00 · on screen: The shared pipeline from designer intent to the comparison and revision interface, the three emphases marked, the rule that the language model does not calculate, and a bounded first case.*

What interests me is not asking an AI to generate a final building. I want to study the system between the designer’s intention and the final decision: how the AI translates an intention into editable geometry, calls the right analysis tools, brings the results back, and lets the designer understand and challenge what happened.

The model plans; validated tools calculate. I would start with one Vancouver site, Rhino and Grasshopper, and one or two performance domains.

## 21 · PhD directions · Performance EvidenceGraph Co‑Designer

*121 words · start by 11:46 · on screen: Direction 1: the seven-part system with the evidence graph highlighted, what is new, technical benchmark and designer study, contribution and the work it builds on.*

My strongest starting point is an evidence-aware co-designer. If the AI changes the geometry, the system should know which previous simulation results are no longer valid. It should not confidently explain an old result as if it still belongs to the current design.

So every performance claim would link to its geometry, parameters, weather file, tool version, settings and units. If a designer asks to make a courtyard more open but keep summer comfort, the AI proposes editable changes, the designer approves, Grasshopper updates, the analysis reruns, and the old result is marked stale with a reason.

I would test it first with a benchmark of edits, failed tool calls and stale results, then with designers, against an ordinary chat-and-simulation workflow.

## 22 · PhD directions · Negotiable‑Agency Performance Co‑Designer

*106 words · start by 12:58 · on screen: Direction 2: the seven-part system with the agency controller highlighted, attribution to GenEnv’s Grasshopper MCP modes and ArchSim, three agency conditions, contribution.*

The second direction asks when the AI should act and when it should stop and ask. I want the designer to be able to negotiate the AI’s role instead of giving it one fixed level of autonomy.

Your Grasshopper MCP already has modes like Inspect, Coach and Execute, so the modes themselves are not the contribution. The question is whether permissions can adjust to consequence, reversibility and the strength of the evidence. For example, the AI may explore shading depths freely but must ask before changing the footprint.

I would compare fixed low autonomy, fixed high autonomy and negotiated agency, on real models with real analysis.

## 23 · PhD directions · Multi‑Agent Performance Deliberation Studio

*126 words · start by 14:02 · on screen: Direction 3: the seven-part system with the deliberation and conflict view highlighted, two bounded domains, three deliberation conditions, contribution beyond existing agent role division.*

The third direction treats performance design as a real disagreement between priorities. Instead of hiding that disagreement inside one score, specialist agents would show their evidence and let the designer decide how the trade-off should shape the project.

Multi-agent modelling and simulation already exist, including ArchSim here at UBC, so more agents is not the point. I would start with two domains, for example daylight and energy. If the daylight agent wants a larger opening and the energy agent warns about cooling, the system shows both claims with their simulation results, generates bounded alternatives, and asks the designer how to weigh them.

I would compare a single agent, hidden multi-agent agreement and visible deliberation. It is the most ambitious of the three, and the riskiest technically.

## 24 · PhD directions · Comparing the three directions

*68 words · start by 15:17 · on screen: Side-by-side comparison; Direction 1 marked as the current starting point without being chosen permanently.*

Side by side: the first is about whether evidence stays valid, the second about who holds control, the third about competing objectives. All three use the same platform and Rhino and Grasshopper, and all three end with a human decision.

My strongest current starting point is Direction 1, but I would value your guidance on which direction most closely supports the funded program and the lab’s developing systems.
